items.q: The wall of the trachea (windpipe) and bronchi of man is furnished with a series of incomplete:
items.e: Incomplete cartilaginous rings support the trachea and the larger bronchi while keeping their lumen open. Smaller bronchi have cartilage plates.

items.q: What does not happen during inspiration in man?
items.e: During inspiration the diaphragm contracts and flattens. Its dome-shaped relaxed position is associated with expiration.

items.q: The lateral walls of the chest cavity of man are composed of the:
items.e: The ribs and intercostal muscles form the side walls. The diaphragm forms the floor rather than the lateral walls.

items.q: When the human blood leaves the capillary bed of the tissue, most of the carbon dioxide is in the form of:
items.e: The textbook assigns about 70% of carbon dioxide transport to bicarbonate ions, the largest fraction.

items.q: Which sequence of organs is correct in air passageway of man?
o: nasal cavities larynx pharynx trachea bronchi
nasal cavities pharynx trachea larynx bronchi
nasal cavities pharynx larynx bronchi trachea
nasal cavities pharynx larynx trachea bronchi
items.e: Air passes from the nasal cavities to the pharynx, larynx, trachea and then the bronchi.

items.q: Which part of the air passage way possesses cartilage plates in its wall?
items.e: Cartilage is arranged as plates in the smaller, more distal bronchi. The trachea and proximal bronchi have ring supports; bronchioles lack cartilage.

items.q: Which event is not associated with the activity of expiration?
o: more dome like shape of diaphragm
back ward & down ward movement of rib cage
items.e: Quiet expiration follows relaxation of the diaphragm and intercostal muscles. Diaphragm contraction initiates inspiration.

items.q: Oxygen carrying capacity of blood does not depend upon:
items.e: For carrying capacity expressed per fixed blood volume, the total quantity of blood is not the determining factor. Oxygen pressure, altitude and carbon-dioxide-related changes affect loading; haemoglobin concentration also matters.

items.q: When haemoglobin of the blood is fully saturated with oxygen, the 100cc of blood contains.
items.e: The textbook gives a maximum of about 20 ml oxygen per 100 ml blood; 1 cc equals 1 ml.

items.q: Shifts in water-solute balance are managed primarily by
items.e: The urinary system adjusts water and solute excretion. Hormones help regulate this kidney response.

items.q: Which is the most important mechanism for water loss from the body?
items.e: Under ordinary conditions, urine is the major regulated route of water loss described in this chapter.

items.q: The process that normally exerts the greatest control over the water balance of an individual is
items.e: Kidneys vary the amount of water reabsorbed and the volume and concentration of urine.

items.q: Which of the following does NOT dispose off a type of waste directly to the environment?
items.e: The circulatory system transports wastes to organs that release them outside the body.

items.q: The most toxic substances routinely found in the blood are metabolites of what type of molelcules?
items.e: The intended answer is proteins: amino-group removal produces toxic ammonia. The lesson also identifies nucleic-acid metabolism as a source of nitrogenous waste, so the wording is broader than this single-choice answer.

items.q: Which of the following is the last structure that urine passes through during its excretion from body?
items.e: Urine leaves the bladder through the urethra to reach the exterior.

items.q: The process during which potassium and hydrogen ions and some toxic substances are put into urine is called
items.e: Tubular secretion transfers these substances from blood around the tubules into the tubular fluid.

items.q: Kidney health is described in terms of
items.e: Filtration rate describes an important aspect of kidney function; it is the relevant measure among the listed options.

items.q: Why is there no glucose present in the filtrate in the distal tubule of a nephron?
o: its molecules are too large to pass across the basement membrane
it is removed by osmosis from the tubule
it is passively absorb by the cells lining the descending the loop of Henle
it is actively absorb by the proximal tubule cells
items.e: Under normal conditions, filtered glucose is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule before the fluid reaches the distal tubule.

items.q: In case of overheating, the body temperature is regulated by:
items.e: The intended response combines greater evaporative cooling through sweating with conservation of water by reducing urine output.

items.q: An animal that warms itself mainly by absorbing heat from its surroundings is known as:
items.e: An ectotherm relies mainly on environmental heat to raise its body temperature.

items.q: The disorder in which bones are porous and thin but bone composition is normal is;
items.e: Osteoporosis involves loss of bone mass and deterioration of its structure, making bones thinner and more fragile.

items.q: The organic portion of bone’s matrix is important in providing all but;
items.e: Organic collagen contributes flexibility and tensile resistance; mineral salts provide the characteristic hardness.

items.q: The remodeling of bone is a function of which cells?
items.e: Osteoclasts resorb old bone and osteoblasts form new bone during remodeling.

items.q: In skeletal muscle, calcium facilitates contraction by binding to
items.e: Calcium binds troponin, allowing tropomyosin to shift and expose actin’s myosin-binding sites.

items.q: Which of the following statements concerning the role of Ca⁺² in the contraction of skeletal muscle is correct?
o: The mitochondria act as a store of Ca⁺⁺ for the contractile process
Ca⁺² entry across the plasma membrane is important in sustaining the contraction of skeletal muscle
A rise in intracellular Ca⁺² allows actin to interact with myosin
The tension of a skeletal muscle fibre is partly regulated by G proteins muscle
items.e: Increased calcium in the muscle-fibre cytoplasm permits the actin–myosin interaction through the regulatory proteins.

items.q: The function of the T tubules in muscle contraction is to
o: release Ca⁺² into the cell interior and then pick it up again
make the action potential deep into the muscle cells
to hamper the the nerve impulse
items.e: T tubules conduct the action potential into the fibre; the sarcoplasmic reticulum stores, releases and takes up calcium.

items.q: The sites where the motor nerve impulse is transmitted from the nerve endings to the skeletal muscle cell membranes are the:
items.e: A neuromuscular junction is the communication site between a motor neuron and a skeletal muscle fibre.

items.q: Myoglobin has a special function in muscle tissue.
o: it holds a reserve supply of oxygen in the muscle
items.e: Myoglobin binds oxygen and provides a reserve in muscle cells.

items.q: Which of the following is common to all neurons?
o: A cell body which contains a nucleus
items.e: Every neuron has a cell body (soma) with a nucleus; myelin, Schwann cells and nodes of Ranvier occur only on myelinated fibres (section 17.2).

items.q: What will occur if a drug at the neuromuscular junction blocks the receptor sites on the post-synaptic membrane?
items.e: If receptors are blocked, the neurotransmitter cannot depolarize the muscle membrane, so the muscle cannot be stimulated to contract (section 17.4.3).

items.q: The groups of ribosomes present in the cell body of the neuron, which are associated with rough endoplasmic reticulum are called:
items.e: Section 17.2 defines Nissl's granules as groups of ribosomes associated with rough ER in the cell body.

items.q: The mammalian forebrain is differentiated into the thalamus, limbic system and the:
items.e: The forebrain contains the cerebrum (telencephalon) together with the thalamus and limbic structures; the cerebellum belongs to the hindbrain (section 17.5.4).

items.q: Information back from the control center to the effectors as done by ________ nerve path way.
items.e: Pathways carrying impulses away from the CNS to effectors are efferent (motor).

items.q: The number of human spinal nerves is:
items.e: The text gives thirty-one pairs of spinal nerves, i.e. 62 nerves (section 17.5.4).

items.q: The electrical potential of cell membrane of neuron when it is not transmitting any signal is called ________.
items.e: A neuron that is not conducting has its resting membrane potential of about −70 mV (section 17.3.1).

items.q: Which one of the following condition is resulted from excess GH in adults?
items.e: Section 18.2.2: over secretion of GH in adult life causes acromegaly.

items.q: ________ regulates the kidney's retention of water.
items.e: ADH (vasopressin) acts on kidney tubules to enhance water reabsorption.

items.q: Which of the following hormones is not released by the anterior pituitary?
items.e: GnRH comes from the hypothalamus (section 18.2.2). Note: the book places MSH in the intermediate lobe, but GnRH is the intended answer.

items.q: Parathyroid hormone acts to ensure that
o: calcium levels in the blood never drop too low
sodium levels in urine are constant
potassium levels in the blood don't escalate
the concentration of water in the blood is sufficient
items.e: Parathormone release is triggered by low blood Ca²⁺ and raises blood calcium (section 18.2.4).

items.q: The adrenal cortex produces ________.
items.e: Aldosterone is the chief mineralocorticoid of the adrenal cortex (section 18.2.6).

items.q: Oxytocin is secreted by the endocrine gland named:
items.e: Oxytocin is stored in and released from the posterior pituitary (section 18.2.2).

items.q: Deficiency of vasopressin or ADH by the pituitary gland leads to a disorder in which the patients kidneys have lessened ability to absorb water is:
items.e: Lack of ADH causes diabetes insipidus, with large volumes of dilute urine.

items.q: The function(s) of oxytocin is/are to ________.
o: stimulate the release of milk from the mother's mammary glands when her baby is nursing.
items.e: Section 18.2.2 lists labour contractions and the milk-ejection reflex.

items.q: In humans, MSH (melanocyte-stimulating hormone) ________.
o: causes the thyroid to produce thyroxin
items.e: MSH stimulates melanin production by melanocytes, darkening the skin (section 18.2.2).

items.q: Innate behavior is all but;
items.e: Section 19.2 lists innate behaviour as inflexible, not flexible.

items.q: Innate behavior is all except:
items.e: Innate behaviour is not modified by development or experience during an individual life (section 19.2).

items.q: Which one is non-directed orientation?
items.e: Section 19.2.2: a kinesis is non-directed orientation.

items.q: Trial and error learning has no role in
items.e: Insight learning solves problems through mental trials rather than trial and error (section 19.3.5).

items.q: Advantage of pecking orders is to
o: avoids injury to the stronger animals
Assign specific role to individual subordinates.
items.e: Section 19.4.4: the pecking order avoids injury to the stronger animals.

items.q: Gonadotropin releasing hormone is responsible for the stimulation/release of which hormone?
items.e: GnRH controls release of the gonadotropins FSH and LH (section 20.1.8).

items.q: Fertilization of the ovum normally occurs:
o: In the upper third of the oviduct
In the lower third of the oviduct
Can take place successfully in vagina
items.e: The oviduct is the site where fertilization generally occurs (section 20.2.2), usually in its upper part near the ovary.

items.q: The human egg is swept through the oviduct toward the uterus by
o: The beating of the eggs' cilia.
The beating of the cilia in the oviduct.
items.e: Section 20.2.2: muscular peristalsis together with beating cilia of the oviduct carry the oocyte; the egg itself has no cilia.

items.q: Embryo implants in the ________ of the uterus
items.e: The young embryo implants in the endometrium (section 20.2.3).

items.q: Which will occur as a result of nondescent of the testes?
o: Male sex hormones will not be circulated in the body.
Sperm will have no means of exit from the body.
Inadequate blood supply will retard the development of the testes.
Viable sperm will not be produced.
items.e: Testes need a temperature below core body temperature (about 35°C) for sperm development (DO YOU KNOW box).

items.q: The corpus luteum is formed at the site of
items.e: After ovulation the ruptured follicle becomes the corpus luteum (section 20.2.1).

items.q: Within the ovary, progesterone is produced by the
items.e: Progesterone comes from the corpus luteum (section 20.3.3).

items.q: The basic difference between spermatogenesis and oogenesis is that
o: during spermatogenesis two more polar bodies are produced.
the mature ovum is haploid while the sperm is 2n.
spermatogenesis involves mitosis and meiosis, but oogenesis involves meiosis only.
in oogenesis, one mature ovum is produced, and in spermatogenesis four mature sperm are produced.
items.e: One primary oocyte yields one ovum plus polar bodies, while one primary spermatocyte yields four sperm.

items.q: The uterine layer which is shed with each monthly cycle is
items.e: The functional layer of the endometrium is shed during menstruation (section 20.3.1).

items.q: The protective coat which surrounds the embryo is known as:
items.e: The amnion forms a fluid-filled sac all around the embryo (section 21.1.2).

items.q: The outer layer of the blastocyst, which later attaches to the uterus, is the
items.e: The trophoblast is the outer cell layer of the blastocyst and takes part in implantation and placenta formation (section 21.1.1).

items.q: Identical twins result from the fertilization of;
items.e: Section 21.3.4: identical twins come from a single egg fertilized by one sperm.

items.q: The most important hormone in initiating and maintaining lactation after birth is;
items.e: Prolactin prepares and maintains milk production; oxytocin causes milk ejection (Unit 18).

items.q: Blood group B phenotype contains anti-A antibodies in the serum and agglutinates any RBC with antigen:
items.e: Group B serum carries anti-A antibodies (Table 22.2), so it agglutinates red cells bearing antigen A.

items.q: Chances for a son or daughter in human birth are:
items.e: XY – XX type: half the sperms carry X and half carry Y, so the sex ratio is 1:1 (section 22.7.1).

items.q: The number of linkage group in man is:
items.e: Linkage groups equal the number of homologous chromosome pairs; humans have 23 pairs (section 22.6.1).

items.q: A man of blood group A marries a woman of blood group B and they have one child. Which one of the following statements about the child's blood is correct?
o: It could be group A only
It could be group AB only
It could be group A or Group B only
It could be any of the groups A, B, AB, O.
items.e: If the parents are Iᴬi and Iᴮi, the child can be IᴬIᴮ (AB), Iᴬi (A), Iᴮi (B) or ii (O) (section 22.3.3).

items.q: How many different kinds of gametes will be formed by an individual, who is heterozygous for four gene pairs:
items.e: Independent assortment gives 2ⁿ kinds of gametes; for four heterozygous pairs 2⁴ = 16.

items.q: A woman with normal colour vision, whose father was red-green colour blind, married a red-green colour-blind man. What is the probability of her first-born child being red-green colour blind?
items.e: She is a carrier (X^C X^c) and he is X^cY: half the daughters (X^cX^c) and half the sons (X^cY) are colour blind, so the probability is 0.50 (section 22.8.6).

items.q: Two parents, each of blood groups A, have a daughter of blood group O. What is the probability that their next child who has blood group O?
items.e: An O daughter shows both parents are Iᴬi; Iᴬi × Iᴬi gives ii with probability 1/4 = 0.25 (product rule, section 22.1.8).

items.q: What are the phenotypes of the parent of a colour-blind son and non-carrier daughter with normal colour vision? (Father / Mother)
items.e: The son received X^c from his mother, so she is at least a carrier; a non-carrier daughter received a normal X from the father, so he is normal (sections 22.8.3 and 22.8.6).

items.q: When expression of a biological character is observed in variable intensity it is due to the affect of:
items.e: Continuous, graded expression of a trait is caused by polygenes with additive effects (section 22.5.3).

items.q: Inheritance of skin colour in man is controlled by eight pairs of genes, which are:
items.e: Skin-colour polygenes lie at different loci and assort independently (section 22.5.5). Note: the text of 22.5.5 says at least three genes, while this question prints "eight pairs".

items.q: A chromosome with unequal length of its arms is called:
items.e: A submetacentric chromosome has its centromere slightly away from the centre, giving one short and one long arm (section 23.1.2).

items.q: In Hershey & Chase experiment, ³²P labeled bacteriophages allowed to infect the bacteria. During analysis ³²P activity was detected:
o: On the surface of bacterial cell
items.e: ³²P-labelled phage DNA was injected into the bacteria, so ³²P was found in the bacterial cells (section 23.4.3).

items.q: In Meselson & Stahl experiment, the DNA from sample at 20 minutes, after centrifugation it made sediments at the:
items.e: After one replication every duplex is a ¹⁴N/¹⁵N hybrid, which forms one intermediate band (section 23.5.4).

items.q: Which of the following act as a stop codon?
items.e: The stop codons are UGA, UAG and UAA (section 23.6.4).

items.q: In mitochondria UGA codon act to specify ------- instead stop codon:
items.e: In mitochondrial DNA, UGA codes for tryptophan (table in section 23.6.4). Option spellings are as printed.

items.q: If the amount of adenine in DNA of a bacterial cell is 36% of the total nitrogenous bases, what will be the amount of guanine in the DNA of a cell in next generation:
items.e: A = T = 36%, so G + C = 28% and G = 14%; semi-conservative replication keeps the base composition the same in the next generation.

items.q: If an mRNA is synthesized with all the different codons, what is the minimum number of amino acids in the protein that is formed by mRNA:
items.e: Of the 64 codons, three are stop codons that code for no amino acid, so at most 61 sense codons can be read; none of the listed numbers is correct.

items.q: In eukaryotic mRNA molecule there are 90 nucleotide involved in translation process. What is the number of amino acid in the protein formed by this mRNA molecule?
items.e: 90 nucleotides make 30 codons; taking the last as the stop codon (which codes for no amino acid) gives 29 amino acids. If the stop codon is not counted among the 90, the answer would be 30.

items.q: In Griffith experiment mice developed pneumonia when they were injected with:
o: heat killed S-type bacteria along with live R-type bacteria.
items.e: Live R-type bacteria were transformed by material from heat-killed S-type bacteria (section 23.4.1). Option (c) "bases" is printed as such.

items.q: If the codon consisted of only two nucleotides, there would be how many possible codons?
items.e: With four bases and two positions there are 4² = 16 possible codons.

items.q: The random loss of alleles in a population is called
items.e: Genetic drift is the chance change (including loss) of allele frequencies in small populations (section 24.5.4).

items.q: Human appendix, coccyx and nictitating membrane of the eye are:
items.e: These reduced, non-functional organs are listed as vestigial organs (evidence 3).

items.q: The existing species are the modified descendants of pre- existing ones according to:
items.e: Descent with modification from pre-existing species is the theory of organic evolution.

items.q: Using the Hardy-Weinberg Principle, which expression represents the frequency of the homozygous recessive genotype?
items.e: q² is the predicted frequency of homozygous recessive (aa) individuals (section 24.5.3).

items.q: Which one of the following would cause the Hardy-Weinberg principle to be inaccurate?
o: The size of the population is very large.
Individuals mate with one another at random.
There is no source of new copies of alleles from outside the population.
items.e: Natural selection changes allele frequencies, so equilibrium no longer holds (section 24.5.3).

items.q: The study of birds is:
items.e: Ornithology is the study of birds.

items.q: Similarity in characteristics resulting from common ancestry is known as:
items.e: Homology is similarity due to shared ancestry and developmental pathways (section 24.5.2). The question number "vi" is printed twice.

items.q: The parts of the body use extensively to cope with the environment become larger and stronger, while those that are not used deteriorate was argued by:
items.e: This use-and-disuse idea is Lamarck's (section 24.3). None of the three printed options is correct; option (d) is missing from the printed page.

items.q: Which one of the following pairs represents analogous features?
items.e: Insect and bat wings do the same job but differ in origin and structure, so they are analogous (section 24.5.2).

items.q: In which of the following situations would evolution be slowest for an inter breeding population? (Migration / Selection Pressure / Variation due to Mutation)
items.e: With no gene flow, little selection and little new variation, allele frequencies change least.

items.q: Which of the following ideas was not part of Charles Darwin's theory of evolution by natural selection?
o: Organisms produce more offspring than the environment can support.
Variation between individuals arises by gene mutation.
Only those individuals that are best adapted to the environment survive and reproduce.
Individuals compete for space and resources.
items.e: Darwin did not know about genes or mutation; the genetic basis of variation was added later by Neo-Darwinism (section 24.5).

items.q: The type of gel most commonly used for short fragment DNA electrophoresis is:
items.e: Polyacrylamide gives high resolution of short DNA fragments (section 26.5.2).

items.q: Cell suspension culture of Cinchona ledgeriana produce:
items.e: Cinchona ledgeriana cell suspension cultures produce quinine (section 26.8.2).

items.q: Dideoxy ribonucleoside triphosphates are used to terminate DNA synthesis at different site. Which method involves this procedure?
items.e: Sanger's chain-termination method uses ddNTPs (section 26.5.1). Option spellings are as printed.

items.q: The gene of choice can also be synthesized in the laboratory from mRNA, using reverse transcriptase. This DNA molecule is called:
items.e: DNA copied from mRNA by reverse transcriptase is complementary DNA (cDNA).

items.q: The enzyme DNA polymerase can work only in
items.e: DNA polymerase adds nucleotides to a 3'-OH end, so synthesis runs 5' to 3' (Unit 23, section 23.5.5).

items.q: In recombinant DNA technology a plasmid vector is cleaved by
o: The same enzyme that cleave the donor DNA
The different enzyme other than that cleave the donor DNA
items.e: The same restriction enzyme gives matching sticky ends on the vector and the donor DNA.

items.q: Thermus aquaticus is the source of
items.e: Taq polymerase is isolated from Thermus aquaticus (section 26.3.1). "polumerase" is printed as such.

items.q: The complete set of chromosomal and extrachromosomal genes of an organism is called:
items.e: The genome is the full set of an organism's genes (section 26.7).

items.q: A totipotent cell means:
o: An undifferentiated cell capable of developing into a system or entire plant
An undifferentiated cell capable of developing into an organ
An undifferentiated cell capable of developing into complete embryo
Cell which lacks the capability differentiate into an organ or system
items.e: Totipotency is the ability of a single cell to regenerate a whole plant, the basis of tissue culture (section 26.8).

items.q: Which of the following is not included in integrated disease management?
items.e: Media awareness and vaccination/medication are both part of integrated disease management (section 27.1), so none of them is excluded.

items.q: BCG vaccine is a type of:
items.e: Table 27.1 lists BCG as a live vaccine.

items.q: Study of proper utilization of economically important domestic animals, it is called:
items.e: Section 27.4: when animal husbandry incorporates proper utilization of economically important domestic animals it is called livestock management.

items.q: Holstein Friesian was imported from Holland. This is by far the best diary breed among exotic cattle regarding milk yield. On an average it gives:
items.e: The FYI box in section 27.4.3 gives an average of 25 litres per day.

items.q: ایوب خان نے بھارت کے ساتھ تاشقند ۔۔۔۔۔ معاہدہ کیا۔
items.e: تاشقند معاہدہ 1966ء میں پاکستان اور بھارت کے درمیان امن معاہدہ تھا۔

items.q: سیاست میں ۔۔۔۔۔ اور رواداری کا رواج عام کرنے کی ضرورت ہے۔
items.e: جمہوری سیاست اختلاف کے ساتھ برداشت اور رواداری کا تقاضا کرتی ہے۔

items.q: وزیر اعظم اور وزراء ۔۔۔۔۔ کے سامنے جواب دہ ہوتے ہیں۔
items.e: پارلیمانی نظام میں وزیر اعظم اور کابینہ پارلیمنٹ کے سامنے جواب دہ ہوتے ہیں۔

items.q: صدرِ پاکستان سپریم کورٹ سے کسی قانونی ضابطے کی ۔۔۔۔۔ کے لیے کہہ سکتے ہیں۔
items.e: آئینی طریقہ کار کے تحت صدر کسی اہم قانونی سوال پر سپریم کورٹ کی رائے طلب کر سکتے ہیں۔

items.q: فوج کی سب سے اہم ذمہ داری ملکی ۔۔۔۔۔ کی حفاظت ہے۔
items.e: مسلح افواج کی بنیادی ذمہ داری ملکی سرحدوں اور دفاع کا تحفظ ہے۔

items.q: Which three parts make up Maple software?
items.e: Maple consists of the user interface, kernel, and library.

items.q: What does the Maple user interface handle?
o: Input, output display, and worksheet control
items.e: The interface handles mathematical input, command input, output display, and worksheet control.

items.q: What is the Maple kernel described as?
items.e: The kernel is a small collection of compiled C code that performs the core calculations.

items.q: What is found in the Maple library?
items.e: The library contains routines for algebra, statistics, calculus, graphics, and other topics.

items.q: Which symbols can terminate a Maple calculation command?
items.e: A Maple calculation statement is followed by a semicolon or a colon.

items.q: What happens when a command has no semicolon or colon?
o: The next input continues the command
items.e: Without a terminator, Maple treats the next command line as a continuation.

items.q: Which operation is performed first in Maple precedence?
items.e: Exponentiation is performed before multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction.

items.q: Which command requests a floating-point evaluation?
items.e: evalf evaluates an expression using floating-point arithmetic.

items.q: What does exact arithmetic preserve?
items.e: Maple keeps rational results exact unless a floating-point evaluation is requested.

items.q: Which command clears Maple's stored session values?
items.e: The restart command returns Maple to its startup state and resets assigned values.

items.q: What file extension is named for the Save command in the book?
items.e: The book instructs the reader to retain the .m extension when saving a variable file.

Which Maple command plots a two-dimensional function?
items.e: The book uses the plot command for two-dimensional graphs.

items.q: In plot(f(x), x=a..b), what does a..b specify?
items.e: The interval a..b specifies the domain over which the function is plotted.

items.q: Which syntax represents a parametric plot in Maple?
items.e: A parametric plot supplies the x and y functions and the parameter interval.

items.q: For y=sec(x), where are the vertical asymptotes?
items.e: sec(x)=1/cos(x), so vertical asymptotes occur where cos(x)=0: x=π/2+kπ.

items.q: What is the default value of the adaptive plotting option?
items.e: Adaptive plotting is true by default.

items.q: Which options control the initial sampling of a plotted function?
items.e: The text explains that sample and numpoints control the interval sampling.

items.q: Which is a valid axes option?
items.e: The axes option can be boxed, framed, none, or normal.

items.q: What does the annotation option add to a plot?
o: Descriptive text attached to a curve or point
items.e: Annotation adds descriptive text to a two-dimensional curve or point plot.

items.q: What is the default setting for gridlines?
items.e: The book states that gridlines are false by default.

items.q: What are default axis labels when variables are available?
items.e: By default, labels are the names of variables in the plotted function.

items.q: When is a legend useful?
items.e: A legend can list an entry for each curve in a multiple-curve plot.

items.q: Which is one of the listed plot styles?
items.e: The listed styles include line, point, point line, polygon, and polygon outline.

items.q: What is the default minimum number of plotted points?
items.e: The numpoints option specifies the minimum number; its default is 200.

items.q: What range is allowed for plot transparency?
items.e: Transparency is a floating-point value from 0 to 1, inclusive.

items.q: A matrix with 3 rows and 2 columns has what order?
items.e: Matrix order is rows by columns, so the order is 3×2.

items.q: Suppose two motor boats leave from the same point at the same time. If one boat travels north at 15 miles per hour and the other boat travels east at 20 miles per hour. How fast will the distance between them be changing after 2 hours?
items.e: Let x be the eastward distance, y the northward distance and z the separation. After t hours, x = 20t and y = 15t, in miles. The right triangle gives z² = x² + y². Differentiating for t > 0: 2z dz/dt = 2x dx/dt + 2y dy/dt. At t = 2, x = 40 miles, y = 30 miles and z = √(40² + 30²) = 50 miles. Use dx/dt = 20 and dy/dt = 15 miles/hour: dz/dt = (40·20 + 30·15)/50 = 1250/50 = 25 miles/hour. The separation is increasing at 25 miles/hour. Independently, z(t) = √((20t)² + (15t)²) = 25t for t ≥ 0, confirming that rate for every t > 0.

items.q: A single cholera bacterium divides every 0.5 hour to produce two complete cholera bacteria. If we start with a colony of 5,000 bacteria, then after $t$ hours there will be a $A(t) = 5000\,2^{2t}$ bacteria. Find $A'(t)$, $A'(1)$ and $A'(5)$. Interpret the results.

items.e: One doubling every 0.5 hour means 2t doublings after t hours, so A(t) = 5000·2^(2t). This agrees with the source model. For an exponential a^u, the derivative is a^u ln a times u′. Here a = 2 and u = 2t, so u′ = 2. Thus A′(t) = 10000ln2·2^(2t) bacteria per hour, for t ≥ 0 under the population model. At t = 1, 2^(2t) = 4. Hence A′(1) = 40000ln2 ≈ 27,725.887 bacteria/hour, about 27,726. At t = 5, 2^(2t) = 1024. Hence A′(5) = 10,240,000ln2 ≈ 7,097,827.129 bacteria/hour, about 7,097,827. These are instantaneous rates of increase, rather than population counts. The populations themselves are A(1) = 20,000 and A(5) = 5,120,000 bacteria. The exact finite one-hour increase is A(t+1) − A(t) = 3A(t), which differs from the instantaneous derivative 2ln2·A(t).

items.q: Find an equation of the normal line to the curve $x^2\sqrt{y - 2} = y^2 - 3x - 1$ at $(1, 2)$.
items.a: x = 1 on the real endpoint branch.
items.e: The radical makes direct differentiation singular at y = 2. Introduce u = √(y − 2) ≥ 0, so y = u² + 2. The source equation becomes x²u = u⁴ + 4u² + 3 − 3x. At (x,u) = (1,0), differentiation with respect to u gives 2xu xᵤ + x² = 4u³ + 8u − 3xᵤ. Thus xᵤ = −1/3, while yᵤ = 2u = 0. The one-sided tangent slope on the real branch is 0, so the normal is x = 1. This point is an endpoint of the source real branch; it is not justified by substituting y = 2 into a derivative that divides by √(y − 2).

items.q: Write short notes on factorials, permutations and combinations.
items.a: Factorial: for a positive integer $n$, $n! = n(n-1)(n-2)\cdots 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1$ and $0! = 1$; it is the number of ways of arranging $n$ different objects in a row. Permutation: an arrangement of objects in a definite order; the number of permutations of $n$ different objects taken $r$ at a time is $^nP_r = \dfrac{n!}{(n-r)!}$. Combination: a selection of objects in which the order does not matter; $^nC_r = \dfrac{n!}{r!\,(n-r)!} = \dfrac{^nP_r}{r!}$, and $^nC_r = {}^nC_{n-r}$.

items.q: Give in brief the concept of probability.
items.a: Probability is a number between 0 and 1 that measures how likely it is that an event will occur. Classical definition: if an experiment has $n$ equally likely outcomes and $m$ of them favour the event $A$, then $P(A) = \dfrac{m}{n}$. $P(A) = 0$ for an impossible event, $P(A) = 1$ for a sure event, and $P(A) + P(\bar{A}) = 1$. In the relative-frequency view, $P(A)$ is the value approached by the proportion of times $A$ occurs when the experiment is repeated many times.

items.q: Random experiment (ii) sample space (iii) outcomes (iv) event (v) impossible event (vi) sure event.
items.a: Random experiment: an experiment whose result cannot be predicted with certainty although all its possible results are known (tossing a coin). Sample space: the set $S$ of all possible outcomes (for a die $S = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$). Outcome: one possible result of the experiment (a sample point). Event: any subset of the sample space (an even number on a die is the event $\{2, 4, 6\}$). Impossible event: an event that cannot occur, the empty set $\varnothing$, with probability 0. Sure event: an event that always occurs, the whole sample space $S$, with probability 1.

items.q: Mutually exclusive events and not mutually exclusive events.
items.a: Mutually exclusive events cannot occur together: $A \cap B = \varnothing$ and $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)$ (a head and a tail in one toss). Events that are not mutually exclusive can occur together: $A \cap B \neq \varnothing$ and $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)$ (an even number and a number greater than 3 on one throw of a die).

items.q: Independent events and dependent events.
items.a: Independent events: the occurrence of one does not change the probability of the other, so $P(A \cap B) = P(A)\,P(B)$ (two tosses of a coin; draws with replacement). Dependent events: the occurrence of one changes the probability of the other, so $P(A \cap B) = P(A)\,P(B \mid A)$ (draws without replacement).

items.q: Define equally likely events, compound events, and exhaustive events.
items.a: Equally likely events: events that have the same chance of occurring, so none is preferred (the six faces of a fair die). Compound event: an event made up of two or more simple events (sample points), e.g. an even number on a die is $\{2, 4, 6\}$. Exhaustive events: events which together make up the whole sample space, so that at least one of them must occur (an even number and an odd number on a die).

items.a: Probability $P(A)$ is the chance of $A$ in the whole sample space. Conditional probability $P(A \mid B) = \dfrac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}$, $P(B) > 0$, is the probability of $A$ given that $B$ has already occurred; the sample space is reduced to $B$.

items.q: State and prove multiplication laws of probability for independent and dependent events.
items.a: Multiplication law for dependent events: $P(A \cap B) = P(A)\,P(B \mid A) = P(B)\,P(A \mid B)$. For independent events: $P(A \cap B) = P(A)\,P(B)$.
items.e: Proof: by definition $P(B \mid A) = \dfrac{P(A \cap B)}{P(A)}$ with $P(A) > 0$; multiplying by $P(A)$ gives $P(A \cap B) = P(A)\,P(B \mid A)$, and in the same way $P(A \cap B) = P(B)\,P(A \mid B)$. If $A$ and $B$ are independent, the occurrence of $A$ does not affect $B$, so $P(B \mid A) = P(B)$ and the law becomes $P(A \cap B) = P(A)\,P(B)$.

items.q: Describe in brief the discrete uniform probability distribution.
items.a: A random variable has a discrete uniform distribution if it takes $N$ values $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_N$, each with the same probability: $p(x) = \dfrac{1}{N}$. For the values $1, 2, \ldots, N$ the mean is $\dfrac{N+1}{2}$ and the variance is $\dfrac{N^2 - 1}{12}$. Example: the number on a fair die, $p(x) = \dfrac{1}{6}$, mean $3.5$.

items.q: What do you know about random digits, random numbers, random number generator and random number table?

items.q: Describe Normal distribution and throw light on the importance of Normal distribution.
items.a: The normal distribution is a continuous, symmetric, bell-shaped distribution with density $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\,e^{-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}}$, $-\infty < x < \infty$, with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$. Importance: many measurements (heights, weights, marks, errors of measurement) follow it closely; the binomial and other distributions are approximated by it when $n$ is large; by the central limit theorem the distribution of sample means is nearly normal for large samples; and it is the basis of estimation and tests of hypotheses.

items.q: Define Normal distribution. Write down its properties.
items.a: The normal distribution of a variable $X$ with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$ has the density $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\,e^{-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}}$. Properties: the curve is bell-shaped and symmetrical about $x = \mu$; mean, median and mode are equal; the total area under the curve is 1; about 68.27% of the area lies within $\mu \pm \sigma$, 95.45% within $\mu \pm 2\sigma$ and 99.73% within $\mu \pm 3\sigma$; the curve never touches the x-axis; the points of inflection are at $\mu \pm \sigma$; skewness is 0.

items.q: Define standard normal variable and standard Normal distribution. What is the role of this distribution?
items.a: A standard normal variable is $Z = \dfrac{X - \mu}{\sigma}$, which has mean 0 and variance 1; its distribution, the standard normal distribution, has density $f(z) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\,e^{-z^2/2}$. Role: any normal probability can be found by changing $X$ into $Z$ and reading the area from the single table of the standard normal distribution.

items.q: What is meant by population, sample and sampling?

items.q: What is the need of sampling as compared to complete enumeration?
items.a: Sampling is needed because complete enumeration (a census) takes much more time, money and labour; for a very large or infinite population it is impossible; when testing destroys the item (testing bulbs, crash tests, blood samples) only a sample can be tested; a small, well-trained team can work more carefully, so the results can be as accurate as a census and are available sooner.

items.q: Sampling and non-sampling errors
items.a: Sampling error: the difference between a sample statistic and the population parameter that arises because only a part of the population is examined; it becomes smaller as the sample size increases. Non-sampling errors: errors that are not caused by sampling but by faulty measurement, wrong recording, non-response, a defective questionnaire or processing mistakes; they occur in a census as well.

items.q: Define parameter, statistic and estimator.
items.a: (a) The main objectives of sampling: to estimate population parameters (mean, proportion, variance) from sample statistics; to test statements (hypotheses) about the population; and to obtain this information reliably at less cost and time than a complete count. (b) Parameter: a numerical measure of a population ($\mu$, $\sigma^2$, $P$). Statistic: a numerical measure calculated from a sample ($\bar{X}$, $S^2$, $\hat{p}$). Estimator: a statistic (a formula or rule) used to estimate a parameter, e.g. $\bar{X}$ is an estimator of $\mu$; the value it takes for a particular sample is an estimate.

items.q: Differentiate between probability and non-probability sampling.
items.a: Probability sampling: every unit has a known, non-zero chance of selection and the sample is drawn by a random method (simple random, stratified, systematic, cluster sampling); sampling error can be measured and the estimates are unbiased. Non-probability sampling: units are chosen by the judgement or convenience of the investigator (judgement, quota, convenience sampling); the chances of selection are unknown and the sampling error cannot be measured.

items.q: Simple random sampling
items.a: Simple random sampling: the sample is drawn so that every unit of the population, and so every possible sample of size $n$, has the same chance of being selected. It is done by a lottery (goldfish bowl) method or with a random number table.

items.q: Stratified random sampling
items.a: Stratified random sampling: the population is divided into non-overlapping groups (strata) of similar units; a simple random sample is drawn from each stratum, for example in proportion to its size ($n_i = n\,\dfrac{N_i}{N}$), and the samples are combined.
items.h: Explain the following methods of selecting a sample:

items.q: Systematic random sampling
items.a: Systematic random sampling: the $N$ units are listed and numbered; the sampling interval $k = \dfrac{N}{n}$ is found; one unit is chosen at random from the first $k$ units, say the $r$-th, and then every $k$-th unit after it ($r, r + k, r + 2k, \ldots$) is selected.
items.h: Explain the following methods of selecting a sample:

items.q: Goldfish bowl method
items.a: A simple random sample is a sample in which every unit of the population has an equal chance of being selected. Goldfish bowl method: write the numbers or names of all units on identical slips, mix them well in a bowl or box, and draw the required number of slips one by one without looking, without replacement.

items.a: The sampling distribution of the difference between two sample means is the distribution of $\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2$ over all pairs of independent samples of sizes $n_1$ and $n_2$ from two populations. items.q: Describe the concept of confidence interval estimation.
items.a: Confidence interval estimation gives an interval $(L, U)$, calculated from the sample, which contains the unknown parameter with a stated probability $1 - \alpha$ (the confidence level, e.g. 95%). items.q: Define hypothesis, statistical hypothesis and testing of hypothesis?
items.a: Hypothesis: a statement or assumption about a population that is to be checked. Statistical hypothesis: a statement about a population parameter or distribution that can be tested with sample data, e.g. $\mu = 50$. Testing of hypothesis: the procedure by which sample information is used to decide whether the hypothesis should be accepted or rejected.

items.q: Explain in your own words (i) Hypothesis testing (ii) Estimation. What are the principle steps involved in hypothesis testing procedure?
items.a: (i) Hypothesis testing: deciding, from sample data, whether a statement about a population is supported or must be rejected. (ii) Estimation: using sample data to find a value or an interval for an unknown parameter. Steps: (1) state the null hypothesis $H_0$ and the alternative hypothesis $H_1$; (2) choose the level of significance $\alpha$; (3) select the test statistic ($Z$, $t$, $\chi^2$, $F$); (4) find the critical region from the table; (5) compute the value of the test statistic from the sample; (6) reject $H_0$ if the value falls in the critical region, otherwise accept (do not reject) it; (7) state the conclusion in words.

items.q: Null and alternative hypothesis.
items.a: Null hypothesis $H_0$: the hypothesis that is tested, stating that there is no difference or effect (e.g. $H_0: \mu = \mu_0$). Alternative hypothesis $H_1$: the statement that is accepted when $H_0$ is rejected ($\mu \neq \mu_0$, $\mu > \mu_0$ or $\mu < \mu_0$).

items.a: Acceptance region: the set of values of the test statistic for which $H_0$ is accepted. Rejection (critical) region: the set of values for which $H_0$ is rejected; its area is $\alpha$ and it is separated from the acceptance region by the critical value(s).

items.a: Test statistic: a quantity calculated from the sample data (such as $Z$, $t$, $\chi^2$ or $F$) whose value is used to decide whether $H_0$ is rejected. Test of significance: the procedure that compares the value of the test statistic with the critical value(s) to decide whether the observed difference is real or due to chance.

items.a: A one-sided (one-tailed) test has a critical region in one tail only: $H_1: \mu > \mu_0$ (right-tailed, reject if $Z \geq Z_\alpha$) or $H_1: \mu < \mu_0$ (left-tailed, reject if $Z \leq -Z_\alpha$). items.q: Describe the general procedure (steps) for testing hypothesis about mean of a normal population when population standard deviation is known and sample size is large.
items.a: Steps: (1) $H_0: \mu = \mu_0$. (2) $H_1: \mu \neq \mu_0$ (or $\mu > \mu_0$, $\mu < \mu_0$). (3) Choose the level of significance $\alpha$. (4) Test statistic $Z = \dfrac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}$. (5) Critical region: $|Z| \geq Z_{\alpha/2}$ for a two-sided test; $Z \geq Z_\alpha$ or $Z \leq -Z_\alpha$ for a one-sided test. (6) Calculate $Z$ from the sample. (7) Reject $H_0$ if $Z$ falls in the critical region, otherwise accept it, and state the conclusion.

Explain hypothesis testing procedure about mean of a normal population when $\sigma$ is unknown and sample size is small.
items.a: Steps (population normal, $\sigma$ unknown, $n$ small): (1) $H_0: \mu = \mu_0$. (2) $H_1: \mu \neq \mu_0$ (or $>$, $<$). (3) Choose $\alpha$. (4) Test statistic $t = \dfrac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{S/\sqrt{n}}$ with $S = \sqrt{\dfrac{\sum (x - \bar{x})^2}{n - 1}}$ and $n - 1$ degrees of freedom. (5) Critical region from the t-table: $|t| \geq t_{\alpha/2,\,n-1}$ (two-sided) or $t \geq t_{\alpha,\,n-1}$ / $t \leq -t_{\alpha,\,n-1}$ (one-sided). (6) Calculate $t$. (7) Reject $H_0$ if $t$ falls in the critical region; otherwise accept it.

items.q: Describe the procedure for testing hypothesis about the equality of means of two normal populations when population standard deviations are known and sample sizes are large.
items.a: Steps: (1) $H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2$ (i.e. $\mu_1 - \mu_2 = 0$). (2) $H_1: \mu_1 \neq \mu_2$ (or $>$, $<$). (3) Choose $\alpha$. (4) Test statistic $Z = \dfrac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{\sqrt{\dfrac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1} + \dfrac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}}}$. (5) Critical region: $|Z| \geq Z_{\alpha/2}$ (two-sided) or $Z \geq Z_\alpha$ / $Z \leq -Z_\alpha$ (one-sided). (6) Calculate $Z$. (7) Reject $H_0$ if $Z$ is in the critical region, otherwise accept it.

items.q: Write the steps used in hypothesis testing about equality of means of two normal populations when $\sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2 = \sigma^2$ but unknown and sample sizes $n_1$, $n_2$ are small.
items.a: Steps: (1) $H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2$. (2) $H_1: \mu_1 \neq \mu_2$ (or $>$, $<$). (3) Choose $\alpha$. (4) Find the pooled variance $S_p^2 = \dfrac{\sum (x_1 - \bar{x}_1)^2 + \sum (x_2 - \bar{x}_2)^2}{n_1 + n_2 - 2}$ and the test statistic $t = \dfrac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{S_p\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{n_1} + \dfrac{1}{n_2}}}$ with $n_1 + n_2 - 2$ degrees of freedom. (5) Critical region from the t-table: $|t| \geq t_{\alpha/2,\,n_1+n_2-2}$ (two-sided). (6) Calculate $t$. (7) Reject $H_0$ if $t$ falls in the critical region, otherwise accept it.

items.q: What is a completely randomized design? What are the merits and demerits of a completely randomized design?
items.a: A completely randomized design (CRD) is a design in which the treatments are allocated to the experimental units completely at random, without any restriction; it is used when the units are homogeneous. Merits: the layout and the analysis are simple; any number of treatments and replications can be used (unequal replication is allowed); a missing observation causes no difficulty; the error has the maximum degrees of freedom. Demerits: it is not suitable for heterogeneous material, because all the variation goes into the error and precision is low; there is no local control.

items.q: Write a short note on analysis of variance.
items.a: Analysis of variance (ANOVA), introduced by R. A. Fisher, divides the total variation of the data into parts due to different sources (variation between the groups or treatments and variation within the groups, the error) and tests with the F-test, $F = \dfrac{\text{mean square between}}{\text{mean square within}}$, whether the means of several populations are equal. The results are shown in an ANOVA table (source of variation, degrees of freedom, sum of squares, mean square, $F$).

items.q: What is meant by analysis of variance? What are the assumptions under which this technique is applied?
items.a: Analysis of variance splits the total variation of the observations into the variation among the group means and the variation within the groups, in order to test $H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2 = \cdots = \mu_k$ with the F-test. Assumptions: (1) the populations from which the samples come are normally distributed; (2) the populations have the same variance; (3) the samples are random and independent; (4) the effects are additive.

items.q: Variance among samples
items.a: Variance among samples (between samples): the variation of the sample means around the grand mean, $SSB = \sum n_i(\bar{x}_i - \bar{x})^2$, and $MSB = \dfrac{SSB}{k - 1}$; it is due to the treatments and chance.

items.q: Variance within samples
items.a: Variance within samples: the variation of the observations around their own sample mean, $SSW = \sum\sum (x_{ij} - \bar{x}_i)^2$, and $MSW = \dfrac{SSW}{N - k}$; it is due to chance (error) only.

items.q: Total variation
